When there shall be less than five players on a side, bounds shall be placed 22 yards each in a line from the off and leg stump. The ball must be hit before the bounds to entitle the striker to a run, which run cannot be obtained unless he touch the bowling stump or crease in a line with his bat, or some part of his person, or go beyond them, and return to the popping crease. When the striker shall hit the ball, one of his feet must be on the ground, behind the popping crease, otherwise the umpire shall call “no hit,” and no run shall be scored. When there shall be less than five players on a side, neither byes, leg-byes, nor overthrows shall be allowed, nor shall the striker be caught out behind the wicket, nor stumped. The fieldsman must return the ball so that it shall cross the ground between the wicket and the bowling stump, or between the bowling stump and the bounds. The striker may run till the ball be so returned. After the striker shall have made one run, if he starts again he must touch the middle stump or crease, and turn before the ball cross the ground to entitle him to another. The striker shall be entitled to three runs for lost ball, and the same number for ball wilfully stopped by a field-man otherwise than with any part of his person. When there shall be more than four players on a side there shall be no bounds. All runs, byes, leg byes, and overthrows shall then be allowed. There shall be no restriction as to the ball being bowled in overs, but no more than one minute shall be allowed between each ball.

The test for the Umpire to apply in deciding if the ball is wide is whether it is within reach of the Striker.
If the striker hit a ball which has been called “Wide” the call should be ignored.
When only one run has been made from a “Wide Ball” the batsmen do not cross over to the positions they were in before the run was made.
This Law should be read with Law 16.
Though provision is made in Law 16 by which the Striker may obtain runs from a “No Ball” the fact remains that “neither a No Ball nor Wide Ball shall be reckoned as one of the over.”
Although not counted in the over No Balls and Wides arc recorded in their proper place on the score sheet.
It is Umpire’s and not the Scorer’s duty to call over.
(See Law 13 and Note.)
When a run is made by the bat off a “NoBall” only the run to the batsman should be scored and not the “No Ball” as well.
If one run is attempted and the batsman is run out the “No Ball” alone counts.
If runs are made off a “No Ball,” although the runs are scored and not the “No Ball,” the bowler is allowed another delivery.
When Byes or Overthrows are run from a “Wide” they are scored as “Wides.”
A Batsman may be out “hit wicket,” when striking at a “Wide.”
It is sufficient if part of the batsman’s foot is grounded within the line.
If the foot is on the line, but no part is within the batsman would be “out of his ground.”
If the batsman is in the act of jumping in the air and the bat is also off the ground he would be “out of his ground.”
If one bail is off it is sufficient to remove the remaining one with the ball in order to stump or run a batsman out.

Although the Law says nothing about the stumps being pulled out it is customary to run a batsman out in this way when the bails are off; but the ball must be in the fieldsman’s hand when he uses it for this purpose.
An Umpire would be justified in giving a batsman out “Bowled” if a stump were bowled down, but the bails by some mischance remained in position.
The ball must not touch the ground before it is held; but the hand holding the ball may touch the ground in effecting the catch.
When a fieldsman catches a ball and falls and the ball touches the ground, it is a question of fact for the Umpire to decide whether or not the catch was completed before the ball touched the ground.
When a Batsman plays a ball on to the ground and in order to prevent it hitting the wicket, after touching the ground, he strikes it again and the ball is caught, the batsman is not out.
But if he hit the ball a second time before it touches the ground and is caught, he would be out under this Law.
A Batsman would be out if caught off a ball which before striking the bat had hit his pad.
If no boundaries have been arranged a Sinker can be caught off a tree, hedge, or building.

If the ball rebounds off the pads or person of the wicket-keeper, without having first touched the bat or hand of the Striker, and the Striker is out of his ground the decision should be “Stumped,” and not “Run Out.”
It is sufficient for the wicket-keeper to remove one bail in order to run out or stump a batsman.
It would not be out if he were to knock the bails off with his foot, or with an arm or hand not holding the ball.
A Batsman may be out l.b.w. although the bowler is bowling round the wicket, if the case comes within this Law.
There are three considerations which an Umpire must bear in mind:— (1)
Would the ball have hit the wicket?
Did it pitch in a straight line between wicket and wicket?
Was it part of the batsman’s person which intercepted the ball?
If these questions are answered in the affirmative the batsman would be out.
It is immaterial whether the ball breaks or not.
It is sometimes only possible for a bowler bowling round the wicket to obtain an l.b.w. with a breaking ball.
(See Law 16, Note 3.)
If in making a second stroke to keep a ball out of his wicket, the Striker hit down his wicket as above he would be out.
A batsman would not be out for breaking the wicket either with his bat or person when in the act of running.
If while playing at the ball, but not otherwise, the Striker’s hat or cap fell on the wicket and dislodged a bail he would be out.
It should be noted that it is the Striker who is out if this Law is infringed.
It is for the Umpire to decide whether the ball has been struck “wilfully” for some purpose other than that of guarding the wicket.
The fact that a run is attempted may be evidence of the batsman’s intention to take advantage of the second stroke and the Umpire is entitled to regard it as such, but it is not conclusive.
If the ball has been lawfully struck twice and an overthrow is made, the batsmen are entitled to the runs which follow.
A Striker may be out for hitting the ball twice, although no run is attempted.
(See Notes to Law 20.)

It would not be out if the striker hit the ball into the opposite wickets —the other batsman being out of his ground—unless the ball had been touched by a fieldsman after being hit and before striking the wickets.
Either batsman can be “run out” at any time when the ball is in play by any fieldsman, including the bowler.
For a definition of “out of his ground” see Law 19 and Notes.
The Umpire must decide on the facts before him if the obstruction was “wilful.”
(Sec Notes on Law 22.)
Although that run which is being attempted shall not be scored it is not the custom for the remaining batsman to resume his position at the wicket he has left if he and his partner have crossed.
A ball can only become “Dead” under Laws 33a, 33b, 34, 35, 41 & 50, or on the call of a boundary hit.
Whether the ball is “finally settled” is a question of fact for the Umpire only to decide.

A bowler may run a Batsman out, without having delivered the ball, in anyway authorized by the Laws, he may have passed the bowling crease in his run or may change the ball from one hand to the other before throwing at the wicket or knocking off the bails.
The bails may be knocked off from either side of the wickets.

It is well to remember that a side which loses a player’s services through illness or injury, brought about during a match, is entitled to a substitute, “it shall be allowed” whereas under other circumstances consent is necessary which must depend upon the courtesy of the opposing Captain.
Many disputes would be avoided if the Captains, before tossing, exchanged lists of the players.
There is no law prohibiting a player from bowling because he has had a substitute to run for him.
A side which has been short in the field may bat with its full number.
The distinction between the words “Striker” and “Batsman” should be appreciated.
When the injured Batsman is not the Striker he is subject to no penalty under this Law.
The “five runs” are to be added to the runs already made when the Fieldsman “wilfully” stopped the ball.
A Wicket-keeper may run a Batsman out by going in front of the Wicket (Law 28) the Umpire must decide from the facts, if the act is legal.
(See also Instructions to Umpires.) 14
It is the duty of the Captains to see that this Law is strictly observed.
N.B.—An appeal, “How’s that?” covers all ways of being out (within the jurisdiction of the Umpire appealed to), unless a specific way of getting out is stated by the person asking.
When the Umpire at the bowler’s wicket has given a Batsman “not out” the other umpire may answer any appeal within his jurisdiction, subject to an observance of Law 50.
If an Umpire has called “No Ball” when the ball has not been delivered he should revoke his decision.
(See Notes under “The Batsman,” page 16.)
No act on the part of the fielding side can cause a batsman to be out after the Umpire has called “Over,” but an appeal may be made within the allotted time. 15
N.B.—A tie is included in the words “played out.”
